perf: Nobody knows for sure what this painting *means.*
Not the kings who owned it.
Not the monks who guarded it.
Not the scholars who have spent their lives on it.
The man who painted it left no letters,
people have looked into this garden
This is the story of The Garden of Earthly Delights,
and of everyone who tried to read it.
His name was Jheronimus van Aken.
So were most of his uncles.
he joined the Brotherhood of Our Lady,
He signed a few of his paintings
with the name of his town.
And that is almost all we know.
Not one word about his own work.
Just a few lines in the town records,
and in the brotherhood's account books.
About twenty-five paintings are confidently his today.
This is the most famous of them.
more than three metres wide when it's open.
it doesn't look strange at all.
It is the third day of Creation.
Up in the corner sits God,
with a book on his lap.
Across the top, two lines from the Psalms.
For he spake, and it was done.
For he commanded, and they were created.
The museum says Bosch first painted a different scene here,
A monster with the head of a bird
A pig in a nun's veil
trying to get him to sign a document.
And in the middle of it all,
a man made of tree trunks and a broken shell,
One historian thought that face might be Bosch himself.
Strange buildings standing in the water.
People have been arguing about it ever since.
The first time anyone writes about this painting
is travelling through Europe with his master.
they visit the palace of Count Henry the Third of Nassau.
In his journal, de Beatis notes
that there are some panels on which bizarre things have been painted.
the Count had it made because he liked to hold frequent banquets
and to see his guests get drunk.
So what was the painting for?
Some historians think it was made for a wedding.
Others think that famous bed was really a ceremonial platform,
that the painting hung in a hall for councils and court hearings,
The Prado believes the triptych was ordered by Henry's uncle,
and named his nephew as his heir.
The Netherlands are ruled by the King of Spain.
And William becomes the leader of the revolt against him.
The Duke gives it to his son Fernando,
When Fernando dies, his things are sold.
the buyer is the king himself.
Philip is the most Catholic king in Europe.
he sends the Garden to his new monastery-palace,
The record of the gift describes
a painting of the variety of the world.
And it gives the name people knew it by.
that Bosch's pictures are tainted with heresy.
is about the vanity of pleasure.
like the taste of a strawberry,
And he writes the line people still quote about Bosch.
show people as they look on the outside.
The Garden stays at the Escorial
for more than three hundred years.
He claims Bosch secretly belonged to a sect of heretics,
and that the painting was made for their grand master.
But most scholars have turned away from it.
Bosch was a member of a Catholic brotherhood
And his greatest collector was the king
Today, the museum reads the middle panel
given over to the sin of lust.
Between the first sin on the left,
and its punishment on the right.
A twenty-year-old music student in Oklahoma,
is looking at the Hell panel late one night.
a sinner lies pinned under a giant lute.
She turns them into modern notation,
But music historians point out a few problems.
Scholars had written it out back in 1961,
and a band had recorded it in 1978.
nobody can say which notes those are.
Bosch painted the same kind of make-believe music
It has the look of music.
I think Bosch may have just been slapping notes up there
to make it look like music.
and every one of them found something different.
And in the middle of the garden,
two owls stare straight out of the painting.

facts.claim: No title was given to the work at the time; the modern title is later; Bosch left no letters or diaries; he did not date his paintings
Bosch born Jheronimus van Aken c. 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch; grandfather Jan van Aken a painter, four of his five sons painters; father Anthonius
Joined the Brotherhood of Our Lady in 1486/7, a devotional confraternity of about 40 influential citizens
Signed several works 'Jheronimus Bosch'; surname from his town; known only from municipal records and the Brotherhood's account books
About 25 paintings confidently attributed to Bosch today
Triptych of oak panels; height 185.8 cm, centre 172.5 cm wide, wings 76.5 cm each (open c. 3.25 m); dated 1490–1500 by the Prado
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

facts.claim: Outer panels in grisaille: Third Day of Creation, vegetation but no human or animal life; tiny God with a Bible on his lap; Psalm 33:9 and 148:5 inscriptions 'For he spake, and it was done' / 'For he commanded, and they were created'
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

facts.claim: Left panel: God presenting Eve to Adam; Bosch first painted the Creation of Eve and changed it (Prado)
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

facts.claim: Right panel 'musical Hell' with instruments of torture; tavern inside the tree-man; Belting proposed the tree-man's face as a self-portrait
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

facts.claim: Bird-headed monster on a throne/toilet eating corpses and excreting them; pig in a nun's veil trying to get a man to sign legal documents

Centre panel: nude figures, oversized animals and fruit, pool with riders, broken structures in the water; Prado: 'two different types of owl that evoke evil' (both owls face the viewer, visible in the painting)
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

facts.claim: Bosch died 9 August 1516; the triptych is first documented in 1517 in Henry III of Nassau's Brussels palace
Antonio de Beatis, secretary to Cardinal Luigi d'Aragona, travelled 1517–18; in the Nassau palace he wrote 'there are some panels on which bizarre things have been painted'
De Beatis on the great bed: 'the Count had it made because he liked to hold frequent banquets and to see his guests get drunk' (Hale tr.)
Possibly commissioned for a wedding (Harbison)
The 'bed' was probably a lit de justice (ceremonial platform); the triptych likely hung in a hall for councils and court hearings, as an exemplum iustitiae (Koldeweij 2023)
Engelbert II of Nassau commissioned it (Prado; Stedelijk Museum Breda); he died 31 May 1504 and named his nephew Henry III his successor
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://stedelijkmuseumbreda.nl/en/see-do/de-lusten-van-engelbrecht/research ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engelbert_II_of_Nassau

facts.claim: Provenance: René de Châlon 1538–44, William I of Orange 1544–67 (Henry's nephew); expropriated in Brussels by the Duke of Alba, 28 May 1568; to Alba's illegitimate son Fernando de Toledo; taken to Spain
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

facts.claim: Philip II bought it at Fernando de Toledo's posthumous sale in 1591; sent to El Escorial 8 July 1593
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

facts.claim: Philip II, 'the most orthodox Catholic of them all', acquired many Bosch paintings
1593 gift record: a painting 'depicting the variety of the world', known as 'Del Madroño' (strawberry tree)
Late-16th-century evidence that some Spaniards thought Bosch's works tainted with heresy; Sigüenza refuted it

Fray José de Sigüenza (1544–1606), librarian and historian (later prior) of El Escorial, History of the Order of St Jerome c. 1605; called it the 'strawberry plant', about the vanity and transient taste of strawberries
Sigüenza: others paint men as they appear outside; Bosch has the courage to paint them as they are inside
At El Escorial for over 340 years before moving to the Prado (1933 per the Prado's provenance; 1939 per Wikipedia)
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

facts.claim: Wilhelm Fraenger (1947): centre panel a joyful millennial paradise of innocence; Bosch an Adamite; commissioned by the sect's Grand Master
Fraenger's theory gained popularity, many popular books still accept it; scholars have increasingly turned away from it; Bosch a member of the Brotherhood of Our Lady, not an Adamite
Prado: centre panel 'a false Paradise given over to the sin of lust'; sin begins in Eden and is punished in Hell
facts.source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

facts.claim: Feb 2014: Amelia Hamrick, 20, Oklahoma Christian University student (music), late at night, transcribed the notes on a sinner's backside to modern notation, recorded and posted it
Media called it the '500-year-old butt song from Hell'

Earlier transcriptions: Lenneberg 1961, Dixon 1981; recorded by Atrium Musicae (Codex Gluteo) 1978; no clef, so pitch can't be known; faux 'Strichnotation' Bosch also used in the Haywain, the Last Judgement and The Singers in the Egg; music book under the lute
Hamrick: 'I think Bosch may have just been slapping notes up there to make it look like music.'

titles: Nobody Knows What This Painting Means
500 Years of Arguing About One Painting
youtube.description_lead: Hieronymus Bosch left no letters, no diary and no title. For five hundred years, the people who owned and studied The Garden of Earthly Delights have read it as a party, a wedding gift, a sermon against lust, a secret heresy and, in 2014, a song written on a sinner's backside. This is the true story of the painting and of everyone who tried to read it: the Nassau counts in Brussels, the Duke of Alba, Philip II and the monks of El Escorial, Wilhelm Fraenger, and the student who turned the 'butt music' into a viral tune.
